{{Short description|Mathematical structure used in graph theory}}
'''Wilson matrix''' is the following <math>4\times 4</math> matrix having integers as elements:<ref name="Nick1">{{cite web |last1=Nick Higham |title=What Is the Wilson Matrix? |url=https://nhigham.com/2021/06/01/what-is-the-wilson-matrix/ |website=What Is the Wilson Matrix? |date=June 2021 |access-date=24 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nicholas J. Higham and Matthew C. Lettington |title=Optimizing and Factorizing the Wilson Matrix |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |date=2022 |volume=129 |issue=5 |pages=454–465 |doi=10.1080/00029890.2022.2038006 |s2cid=233322415 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00029890.2022.2038006 |access-date=24 May 2022|url-access=subscription }} (An eprint of the paper is available [http://eprints.maths.manchester.ac.uk/2803/3/paper_cropped2.pdf here])</ref><ref name="Cleve">{{cite web |last1=Cleve Moler |title=Reviving Wilson's Matrix |url=https://blogs.mathworks.com/cleve/2018/08/20/reviving-wilsons-matrix/ |website=Cleve’s Corner: Cleve Moler on Mathematics and Computing |publisher=MathWorks |access-date=24 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Carl Erik Froberg |title=Introduction to Numerical Analysis |date=1969 |publisher=Addison-Wesley |location=Reading, Mass. |edition=2}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Robert T Gregory and David L Karney |title=A Collection of Matrices for Testing Computational Algorithms |date=1978 |publisher=Robert Krieger Publishing Company |location=Huntington, New York |page=57}}</ref>

::<math>W = \begin{bmatrix}5&7&6&5 \\ 7&10&8&7 \\ 6&8&10&9 \\ 5&7&9&10\end{bmatrix}</math>

This is the [[coefficient matrix]] of the following [[system of linear equations]] considered in a paper by J. Morris published in 1946:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=J Morris |title=An escalator process for the solution of linear simultaneous equations |journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science |date=1946 |volume=37 |issue=265 |pages=106–120 |doi=10.1080/14786444608561331 |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/14786444608561331 |access-date=19 May 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

::<math> 
\text{(S1)}\quad \begin{align} 
5x+7y+6z+5u & = 23\\
7x+10y+8z+7u & = 32\\
6x+8y+10z+9u&=33\\
5x+7y+9z+10u&=31
\end{align}   
</math>

Morris ascribes the source of the set of equations to one T. S. Wilson but no details about Wilson have been provided. The particular system of equations was used by Morris to illustrate the concept of ill-conditioned system of equations. The matrix <math>W</math> has been used as an example and for test purposes in many research papers and books over the years. John Todd has referred to <math>W</math> as “the notorious matrix W of T. S. Wilson”.<ref name="Nick1"/>

==Properties==
#<math>W</math> is a [[symmetric matrix]].
#<math>W</math> is [[positive definite matrix|positive definite]].
#The [[determinant]] of <math>W</math> is <math> 1</math>.
#The [[Invertible matrix|inverse]] of <math>W</math> is <math>W^{-1} = 
\begin{bmatrix} 68 & -41 & -17 & 10\\ -41 & 25 & 10 & -6 \\ -17 & 10 & 5 &- 3 \\ 10 & -6 & -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
</math>
#The [[characteristic polynomial]] of <math>W</math> is <math> \lambda^4-35 \lambda^3+146 \lambda^2-100 \lambda+1</math>.
#The [[eigenvalues]] of <math>W</math> are <math> \quad 0.01015004839789187,\quad 0.8431071498550294,\quad 3.858057455944953,\quad 30.28868534580213</math>.
#Since <math>W</math> is symmetric, the <math>L^2</math> norm [[condition number]] of <math>W</math> is <math>\kappa_2(W)=\frac{max(\lambda)}{min(\lambda)}=\frac{30.28868534580213}{0.01015004839789187}  = 2984.09270167549</math>.
#The solution of the system of equations <math>(S1)</math> is <math>x=y=z=u=1</math>.
#The [[Cholesky factorisation]] of <math>W</math> is <math>W= R^TR</math> where <math>R
=\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{5} & \frac{7}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}} & \sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}</math>.
#<math>W</math> has the factorisation <math>W= LDL^T</math> where <math>L =
\begin{bmatrix} 
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{5} & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{6}{5} & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1
\end{bmatrix}, 
\quad 
D=\begin{bmatrix} 
5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}
\end{bmatrix} 
</math>.
#<math>W</math> has the factorisation <math>W=Z^TZ</math> with <math>Z</math> as the [[integer]] matrix<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nicholas J. Higham, Matthew C. Lettington, Karl Michael Schmidt |title=integer matrix factorisations, superalgebras and the quadratic form obstruction |journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications |date=2021 |volume=622 |pages=250–267 |doi=10.1016/j.laa.2021.03.028 |s2cid=232146938 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2103.04149 }}</ref> <math>Z=
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 3 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 
\end{bmatrix}
</math>.

==Research problems spawned by Wilson matrix==
A consideration of the condition number of the Wilson matrix has spawned several interesting research problems relating to condition numbers of matrices in certain special classes of matrices having some or all the special features of the Wilson matrix. In particular, the following special classes of matrices have been studied:<ref name="Nick1"/>

#<math>S=</math> the set of <math> 4 \times 4 </math> nonsingular, symmetric matrices with integer entries between 1 and 10.
#<math> P = </math> the set of <math> 4 \times 4 </math> positive definite, symmetric matrices with integer entries between 1 and 10.

An exhaustive computation of the condition numbers of the matrices in the above sets has yielded the following results:

#Among the elements of <math>S</math>, the maximum condition number is <math>7.6119\times 10^4</math> and this maximum is attained by the matrix <math>
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 7 & 10 & 10 \\ 7 & 10 & 10 & 9 \\ 10 & 10 & 10 & 1 \\ 10 & 9 & 1 & 10
\end{bmatrix}
</math>.
#Among the elements of <math>P</math>, the maximum condition number is <math>3.5529 \times 10^4</math> and this maximum is attained by the matrix <math>
\begin{bmatrix}
9 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 10 & 1 & 9 \\ 1 & 1 & 10 & 1 \\  5 & 9 & 1 & 10
\end{bmatrix}
</math>.
